actualProfiles.name: Personal & Professional Development
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
actualProfiles.judgment: Mandatory personal/professional development; not French-language or disciplinary credit.

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
actualProfiles.actualContent: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work.
actualProfiles.judgment: General literary critical reading across fiction/poetry/drama; real methods contribution7.5EC, no French-language sequence.

actualProfiles.name: Great Literary Works
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course is based on a selection of major literary texts which should be considered essential for every LAS student’s cultural capital: texts that for centuries have inspired Western culture, visual arts and theatre, and which resonate themes that preoccupy social sciences and philosophy. The course is a chronological overview of literature ranging from the earliest monuments (the epic of Gilgamesh) to post-modernity. Within this framework students will read primary (literary) and secondary (critical, theoretical) texts debating what it means to be human, mortal, female, male, or child, or what it means to be responsible, free, a member of family or other community, to be civilized or barbarian. What makes literature different from anecdote? Why are some children’s texts indebted to philosophical tale? Probing these and many other questions, students will be invited to analyse literary representations of home, labour, leisure, duty, love, leadership, organized religion, and memory, and try to correlate these topics with various artistic forms used by writers. In this way the course is an encounter with diverse genres: heroic epic, philosophical tale, fairy tale, short story, autobiography, essay and novella. With this broad approach to themes and forms in the Western literary heritage, the course is an alternative introduction to literary studies, and of fundamental value to everyone interested in literary and cultural studies.
actualProfiles.judgment: General Western literary history includes French works; partial7.5EC cultural relevance, no sustained francophone specialisation.

actualProfiles.name: Life & Travel Writing
actualProfiles.actualContent: The course is devoted to various forms of life narrative in literature and popular culture such as memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel narrative as well as blog. It prepares students to read and analyse them, and be sensitive to autobiographical modes in the media. Through this critical encounter with life storying students are encouraged to develop a critical awareness of the postmodern ‘culture of autobiography’ (Folkenflik, R. The Culture of Autobiography. Stanford UP, 1993). In the course, students will build up their writing, presentation and debating skills, and their critical self-reflection. They will be invited to prove their comprehension of crucial theoretical aspects of life narrative research referring to their own individual experience and applying their creative writing skills in order to produce structured personal narratives. With its broadly conceived approach to life narrative studied in the context of large cultural processes, the course ideally fits the paradigm of liberal arts.
actualProfiles.judgment: Life/travel narrative and personal stories; not French-language literature training.

actualProfiles.name: Film & Text
actualProfiles.actualContent: It is a researched fact that more than 50% of films have their literary originals. More than three-quarters of the American Academy Awards have been granted to films based on novels, short stories and dramas. There are plentiful examples of famous films based on no less famous literary texts, from the already hackneyed Pride and Prejudice, through Bridget Jones’ Diary, The Lord of the Rings, the Narnia cycle, A Passage to India, Batman, A Thousand and One Nights to Frankenstein, Dracula, Ninety Eighty-Four and Hamlet. This close relation between literature and film becomes even clearer when we realize that film is a text that tells a story. Keeping this in mind, in this course we will discuss various ways in which a literary original is translated on screen, tracing various links between literary and film narration, and various intertextual dimensions of film adaptation. The course offers instruction in a methodology of film analysis, building on students’ knowledge of literature, media and popular culture. As it studies manifold transactions between the adaptor, the critic and the viewers, it is vital to every student interested in literature, media, popular culture and journalism. Our first step is the basic formalist analysis of a literary text along with its plot, structure, character, setting, and a formalist analysis of the multi-track film (image, acting, music, sound effects) along with its “syntax” and “diction” which all contribute to its tone and themes.
actualProfiles.judgment: Film/text adaptation methods; no guaranteed French film/literature object.

actualProfiles.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
actualProfiles.actualContent: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
actualProfiles.judgment: General literary theory/project across theoretical approaches; not French research formation or a French thesis substitute.

actualProfiles.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
actualProfiles.actualContent: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. The course starts by considering the Greek and Roman Western roots of rhetoric. It focuses on the canons of rhetoric applied to the three main types of argumentation, i.e.
actualProfiles.judgment: General rhetoric, not advanced French speaking/writing.

actualProfiles.name: Style & Meaning
actualProfiles.actualContent: The Style and Meaning course is firmly grounded in stylistics, which is the study of style in texts. Stylistics involves identifying and analysing the linguistic choices that serve to create meaning in texts. Originally an outgrowth of the third canon of classical rhetoric (elocutio), and later heavily influenced by movements in twentieth and twenty-first century linguistics, modern stylistics has grown into a recognizable discipline in its own right, with its own distinct theories and practices. While stylistics can be used to analyse any type of text, traditionally the discipline has been most concerned with the style of literary texts. As such, stylistics has sometimes been referred to as ‘literary stylistics’ or ‘literary linguistics.’ The course textbook also works almost exclusively with fictional texts to introduce and illustrate theoretical concepts and frameworks and their application. Nonetheless, further in-class application will at times extend beyond the fictional and students will be allowed to choose non-fictional texts for their instruction presentations and term papers. Students will be invited to consider the linguistic choices made by (literary) writers by reflecting on why certain linguistic strategies may be more effective than others in achieving particular interpretive effects. Students will be asked to consider all levels of language from the phonetic to the discoursal, to the cognitive. Therefore, an interest in language is crucial to this course.
actualProfiles.judgment: Literary stylistics, largely fictional text analysis; not French proficiency or French linguistics.

actualProfiles.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
actualProfiles.actualContent: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material.
actualProfiles.judgment: Poetry/performance/hybrid creative project; not creative writing in French.

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Sociology
actualProfiles.actualContent: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
actualProfiles.judgment: General sociology support only.

actualProfiles.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
actualProfiles.actualContent: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
actualProfiles.judgment: General qualitative social inquiry; no French disciplinary object.

actualProfiles.name: Theory of International Relations
actualProfiles.actualContent: Brewing wars in the South China Sea, the Middle East, and Europe, trade wars, global climate change, amongst a plethora of other crises and difficulties, show the importance of understanding International Relations and geopolitics. This course gives the student a basic understanding of International Relations through a historical and contemporary scope. You work with a textbook to understand the different schools of thought within International Relations and then use historical or contemporary topics to apply these theories to. This will be achieved by group presentations. Your knowledge will be further increased by homework assignments and an exam. Finally, you end the course with a United Nations Security Council Simulation, where you take on the role of one of the UNSC members, and plead your country’s case in a current problem of international relations.
actualProfiles.judgment: General international relations, not France-specific institutional history or foreign-language study.

actualProfiles.name: European Union Politics
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.
actualProfiles.judgment: EU institutions/dossier research; genuine European-context contribution7.5EC, no French-specific sequence or legal translation.

actualProfiles.name: Modern History
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations.
actualProfiles.judgment: Broad modern history1815onward; no sustained French regional curriculum.

actualProfiles.name: History of Empires
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course is about great powers, superpowers and even hyperpowers. ‘Empire’ is a powerful and dangerous word. It has a rich and ambiguous history and strong polemical connotations now and in the past. The typical empire is usually presented as oppressive and ruthless, although some of the modern empires are democracies that focus upon the improvements of its society. This course deals with some of the most important empires in World History. Next to this some of the most important theories on empires will be treated. How is the rise and fall of empires explained? What are the sources of empire and how are great power politics conducted?
actualProfiles.judgment: Global empires and postcolonial history; no guaranteed francophone regional formation.

actualProfiles.name: History Research Seminar
actualProfiles.actualContent: In the summer of 1809 the British sailed some 40,000 soldiers and 5,000 horses in 500 navy vessels over the English Channel to land in Walcheren. This greatest amphibious operation in Napoleonic times became know as the Walcheren Expedition or the Expedition to the Scheldt. The ultimate British goal was to occupy the important harbour of Antwerp. On the other side, Dutch and French forces, including many foreign troops like Irish, German and Polish were trying to stop the British assault. The outcome of the Walcheren Expedition not only left a big mark on local history, but also had an enormous impact on the Netherlands, France, Great Brittain and international politics in general. In this course we will research the primary sources about the Walcheren expedition. Think about diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports written by soldiers, officers or officials form all participants in this conflict. You will learn how to search for, read and analyse these primary sources, through writing a course-filling paper; as such, this course will require a lot of self-study and fewer class meetings.
actualProfiles.judgment: Walcheren1809 British/French conflict uses primary sources; real narrow French-history contact7.5EC, not sustained French cultural history.

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Film & Media
actualProfiles.actualContent: MCCMED111: Introduction to Film & Media provides you with a solid foundation in the study of film, while also introducing you briefly to media more broadly. The course begins by tracing the development of cinema from its earliest experiments to later artistic movements and innovations. This historical perspective helps you understand film not only as entertainment but also as an evolving cultural form that reflects and shapes society. At the same time, we focus on the elements of film form, such as narrative, cinematography, editing, and sound, which give you the vocabulary needed to describe and analyze how films work. Much of our attention is on film culture and analysis, since these provide the best starting point for further study in the field. Together, we examine and discuss influential examples, considering both their artistic qualities and their broader theoretical and political contexts. This approach allows you to see how films respond to social change while also experimenting with style and technique. In the final part of the course, we widen our perspective to take a short look at media more generally. By considering examples from television, streaming, and digital platforms, we make connections between film and the wider media environment and prepare the ground for more advanced courses in the cluster. Engagement with academic readings is another central part of the course. These texts present important concepts and debates that shape the study of film and media.
actualProfiles.judgment: General film/cultural analysis; no French corpus guaranteed.

actualProfiles.name: Media Archaeology
actualProfiles.actualContent: Media Archaeology explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies, such as cassette tapes, typewriters, and early printed books, and how they shaped the production, circulation, and preservation of knowledge. We will study these objects from multiple perspectives, combining close material analysis with broader historical and cultural interpretation. You will examine how physical properties such as weight, texture, and durability influence communication and memory. The course will include seminar discussions, critical reflections, and hands-on activities that encourage active engagement with obsolete media. Practical exercises may involve recording silence, identifying the sonic characteristics of cassette hiss, or investigating the design, use, and cultural impact of the Sony Walkman. Through these activities, we will learn to treat media as both historical evidence and lived experience, linking material form to cultural meaning. These media objects are chosen because they exemplify the theories and readings central to debates in media archaeology today. By the end of the semester, you will have developed analytical thinking, interpretive skill, and cultural awareness consistent with the aims of a liberal arts education. You will be able to explain how studying obsolete and pre-digital technologies informs our understanding of today’s media. No technical expertise is required, only curiosity and a willingness to work closely with media as physical and cultural artifacts.
actualProfiles.judgment: Pre-digital media history; not French cultural/linguistic training.

actualProfiles.name: The Documentary
actualProfiles.actualContent: In this course we will discuss the development of the documentary form and discover various techniques used by documentary film makers. We start by tracing the documentary film from its origins (e.g. including the work of pioneer documentarians like Dziga Vertov and Robert Flaherty) to the present. We will analyze a large number of non-fiction representations of the world and its people, focusing on a range of documentary styles and genres and rooting this diversity in its various historical and social contexts, as well as considering the ethical and aesthetic aspects of documentaries. The course primarily considers documentary film, but we will also explore the genre through other media forms, including audio productions, allowing students to develop skills useful in an increasingly multimodal culture. Assessment includes a presentation, the production of a very short documentary item, an essay-type exam and several small homework assignments on Moodle. Input to help shape this course is highly appreciated.
actualProfiles.judgment: Documentary making/interpretation; no French regional/language object.

actualProfiles.name: Introduction to Western Art History
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course provides a chronological overview of Western art history from the early Renaissance to the present. It emphasizes key paintings that define specific periods or movements, exploring the works and their creators in detail. The course also considers the impact of art institutions, markets, critics, and historiographers on the legacy of these masterpieces. Focusing on major stylistic movements in Europe and the Americas, the course lays the groundwork for advanced art history studies. It introduces essential tools for visual analysis and interpretation, fostering an understanding of how visual culture reflects historical contexts and societal values.
actualProfiles.judgment: Western art includes French artists; partial relevance7.5EC, not French disciplinary formation.

actualProfiles.name: African Art & Heritage
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course offers an introduction to African art and heritage, with a special focus on the rich artistic traditions of western Africa. Students will study the region’s diverse visual languages, uncovering how sculptures, masks, and other forms of visual expression embody cultural, religious, and social meaning. The course also traces Africa’s enduring influence on global art, from the appropriations of European artists like Picasso and Matisse to modern and contemporary African and African diaspora artists who reinterpret traditional forms in often unexpected ways. A significant component of the course addresses ethical and institutional questions surrounding the collection and display of African art. Through case studies and critical debate, students will explore the legacy of colonial-era looting, the politics of museum acquisitions, and the growing movement for repatriation of African art to their place of origin. Designed for students interested in art history, cultural heritage, and museum studies, the course encourages you to see African art not just as objects, but as living stories: resilient, resonant, and still unfolding.
actualProfiles.judgment: African art/heritage/colonial looting, mainly West African; cannot infer francophone-language/area studies from geography alone.

actualProfiles.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course examines key debates on modern art through a carefully selected range of themes and topics. A central focus is the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions. By exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies, students will gain insight into how art institutions shape public perception and understanding of modern and contemporary art.
actualProfiles.judgment: Modern museums/heritage; no French cultural-history sequence.

actualProfiles.name: Writing Art's Histories
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
actualProfiles.judgment: Art historiography includes Foucault/Derrida; reading French theorists does not establish French-language study. Uses actual enriched description2 fallback.

actualProfiles.name: Philosophy of Emotion
actualProfiles.actualContent: Emotions are a basic aspect of human experience, but they have been, throughout the history of philosophy, contrasted with and sidelined by the pursuit of rationality. They seem to be of important value, central to our well-being, and yet they can often be deeply messy and puzzling. This course provides the opportunity to engage with key questions in the study of emotions from a philosophical perspective. The core topics we shall explore in the course are: (i) The nature of emotions. What are emotions? Are they like beliefs, feelings, or perceptions? (ii) Emotions and ethics. What is the role of emotion in well-being? How important are emotions for moral judgment? In what ways are emotions significant for moral motivation and character? (iii) Emotions and rationality. What does it mean for an emotion to be appropriate? What makes emotions rational or irrational? (iv) Particular emotions: love, fear, disgust; emotions and moods. (v) Emotions and politics. What is the place of the emotions in the context of political projects? Are there emotions we should cultivate as a political community, others we should reject? (vi) Emotions and art. Are we able to experience genuine emotion towards works of fiction? Are there emotions that are specific to the appreciation of art? What is the relation between aesthetic emotions and moral emotions? GOSPHIL311: Philosophy of Emotion We will consider sources from the history of philosophy as well contemporary research on the emotions from philosophy and additional disciplines.
actualProfiles.judgment: Philosophy of emotion with normative/aesthetic inquiry; not French-language/culture formation.

actualProfiles.name: Psycholinguistics
actualProfiles.actualContent: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
actualProfiles.judgment: 7.5EC psycholinguistics/acquisition/neuroscience; useful adjacent language-science content, not French linguistics or French proficiency; prerequisite HCBGATE102.

actualProfiles.name: Dutch
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.
actualProfiles.judgment: Basic Dutch communication/culture, not French.

actualProfiles.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
actualProfiles.actualContent: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.
actualProfiles.judgment: Human rights includes1789French declaration as a historical example; not French law/translation/language sequence.

actualProfiles.name: Principles of Private Law
actualProfiles.actualContent: Life comprises a variety of situations in which private law plays a role . Simply considering the home implicates several complex relationships: family relatives , landlords and tenants, neighbors. Stepping out the front door leads to a further range of transactions that can have legal consequences for those involved. The rights and obligations associated with relationships and transactions among (natural and legal) persons are largely determined by a collection of legal areas known collectively as private law. This course introduces students to principles of selected fields of private law, and students will closely examine property law, tort law, contract law, and other legal areas. The overarching principles within each of these fields will be illuminated using a comparative law approach, considering primarily the legal systems of Germany, France, England, China, and the United States of America. Additionally, students will be challenged to consider private law concepts in broader contexts. Building on the skills acquired in GOSLAWJ101 and other UCR law track courses , this course on private law will seek to uncover the latent social, economic, and political pressures underlying many of the legal principles that will be discussed.
actualProfiles.judgment: Comparative private law includes France among five systems; no French-language legal translation, prerequisite GOSGATE102.
